result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.average_degree_connectivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get the average neighbor degree of nodes, grouped by their own degree. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28447-L28510){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.average_degree_connectivity( source="in+out", target="in+out", weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Average degree connectivity](/assets/graphs/average-degree-connectivity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two hubs C and D of degree 3, linked to each other and to two leaves of degree 1 apiece. Every leaf's neighbor is a hub, so degree 1 maps to 3.0, while the hubs' six neighbors have degrees 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, 1, so degree 3 maps to 1.667: a falling curve, the mark of disassortative mixing." width="100%"} For each degree `k`, the average degree of the neighbors of all nodes with degree `k`, often written `k_nn(k)`. Plotted against `k`, it shows the network's degree mixing at a glance: a rising curve means high-degree nodes link to each other (assortative, as in many social networks), a falling curve means hubs link to low-degree nodes (disassortative, as in many technological and biological networks). It is the degree-resolved version of `get_assortativity_degree()` and the aggregate of `average_neighbor_degree()`. With weights, each neighbor's degree counts in proportion to the weight of the edge to it. Values match NetworkX's `average_degree_connectivity()`, except on directed graphs with `source="in+out"`: NetworkX's documentation describes in- and out-neighbors, but its code averages over successors only while dividing by the total degree. EdgeCase follows the documented definition, counting every incident edge. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["in+out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : On directed graphs, which neighbors to average over and which degree groups nodes: `"out"` (successors, by out-degree), `"in"` (predecessors, by in-degree), or `"in+out"` (default, all neighbors, by total degree). [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["in+out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : On directed graphs, which degree of the neighbors to average: `"in"`, `"out"`, or `"in+out"` (default). [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to weight by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping each degree `k` present in the graph to the average degree of those nodes' neighbors, sorted by `k`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` or `target=` is invalid, or set to something other than `"in+out"` on an undirected graph. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a star, the leaves (degree 1) all point to the hub, while the hub's neighbors are all leaves, the hallmark of a disassortative network: ::: {#314720a5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5).average_degree_connectivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {1: 4.0, 4: 1.0} ``` ::: :::
